title: Welding & Joining
summary: Arc welding processes, weld symbols and joint types, heat input and distortion control, and weld inspection methods.

sections.heading: Welding as a Design Decision
sections.content: Welding fuses parent metal + filler into a **continuous metallurgical joint** — stronger and lighter than bolted joints, but permanent and heat-affected. Welded structures (frames, enclosures, pressure vessels, machinery beds) dominate fabrication because they turn flat stock and sections into rigid, sealed monoliths. The designer's job: choose the process, define the weld with symbols, control distortion, and specify the inspection that proves the weld is sound (see [[sheet-metal-manufacturing|sheet metal]] for the flat-stock world welding belongs to).

sections.heading: Arc Welding Processes
sections.content:
The four main arc processes cover nearly all structural fabrication:

| Process | Principle | Strengths | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| SMAW (stick) | Coated electrode | Simple, portable, cheap | Site work, repair |
| GMAW (MIG) | Continuous wire + gas shield | High rate, easy automation | Production fabrication |
| FCAW | Tubular wire, self/cos-shielded | Fast, outdoor-capable, thick plate | Structural steel |
| GTAW (TIG) | Tungsten arc + separate filler | Cleanest, precise, all metals | Stainless, aluminium, thin, critical |

Selection drivers: material (aluminium → TIG/MIG), thickness (thin → TIG controls heat; thick → FCAW/saw), position (overhead → stick or flux-cored), environment (outdoor wind kills MIG shielding gas), and rate. TIG is the quality king but the slowest; MIG is the volume workhorse; stick is the survivor. **Welder qualification** (e.g. ISO 9606 / AWS D1.1) — the joint is only as good as the qualified welder who made it, and codes require documented qualification.

sections.heading: Weld Symbols & Joint Types
sections.content:
Weld symbols put the entire weld specification on the drawing line (see [[engineering-drawings-and-bom|drawings]]):

- **Reference line + arrow** — arrow points at the joint; the symbol sits on the reference line (near side = arrow side, far side = other side, both sides = above and below the line).
- **Fillet weld** — right-angle triangle symbol: 6 (mm leg size) on the left, length on the right: a 6 mm fillet, 100 mm long on the arrow side.
- **Groove welds** — V, bevel, U, J symbols carry included angle and root opening: a V-groove "60° included, 3 mm root gap" needs **backing or back-gouging** for full penetration.
- **Weld-all-around** (circle at the junction) and field-weld (flag) flags complete the vocabulary.

Joint types: **butt** (full strength potential), **lap/T** (fillet welds, cheap, shear-loaded), **corner/edge** (thin-section enclosures). A fillet weld's throat is 0.707 × leg — the shear check uses the throat: $\tau \approx F/(0.707 \, a \, L)$ for leg $a$ and length $L$. Design rule: put the weld where the load **flows**; an undersized fillet on a stiff frame fails at the first vibration cycle, not under static load.

sections.heading: Heat Input & the HAZ
sections.content:
Heat input controls the **heat-affected zone** (HAZ) — the metal adjacent to the weld that was heated but not melted, where grain growth and hard phases decide properties:

$$H = \frac{V \cdot I}{v} \; [\text{kJ/mm}]$$

Example — 25 V, 200 A, travel speed 5 mm/s:

$$H = \frac{25 \times 200}{5} = 1000 \text{ J/mm} = 1.0 \text{ kJ/mm}$$

- **Too high** → wide HAZ, grain growth, distortion, softened HAZ in work-hardened alloys.
- **Too low** → fast cooling → hard, brittle martensite in steels (cracking risk) and lack of fusion.
- For hardenable steels, **preheat** slows the cooling rate: rule of thumb — preheat ~100 °C for carbon steel above ~25 mm or above ~0.4% carbon; from the carbon equivalent:

$$CE = C + \frac{Mn}{6} + \frac{Cr+Mo+V}{5} + \frac{Ni+Cu}{15}$$

CE > 0.4–0.5 warns "preheat or crack"; the CE is why the same steel grades behave differently across suppliers.

sections.heading: Distortion Control
sections.content:
Welding shrinks as it cools; restrained shrinkage becomes **distortion** (angular, longitudinal, buckling). Since it cannot be eliminated, it must be **managed**:

- **Balance the welds** — weld symmetrically about the neutral axis; sequence the passes to balance contraction (center-out, backstep, skip-weld).
- **Tack and clamp** — fixturing restrains the part during cooling; release only when below ~100 °C to reduce springback.
- **Reduce heat input** — more passes with smaller legs beat one huge pass; intermittent (skip) fillets instead of continuous when sealing allows.
- **Pre-set** — lean the joint opposite the expected distortion so it straightens on cooling.
- **Post-weld straightening** — flame straightening, peening, or thermal stress relief where the code allows.

Rule of thumb: weld **as little as the design allows** — each kilogram of deposited weld metal is a kilogram of potential distortion. Symmetric sections and minimum-leg fillets are the highest-value distortion controls in fabrication.

sections.heading: Weld Inspection & Quality
sections.content:
A weld's internal quality is invisible; inspection is the proof:

- **Visual (VT)** — every weld: size, contour, undercut, porosity on the surface, cracks. Catches most rejects at the cheapest cost.
- **Surface NDT**: **PT** (penetrant — dye, surface cracks), **MT** (magnetic particle — surface/near-surface, ferromagnetic).
- **Volumetric NDT**: **UT** (ultrasonic — thickness, embedded flaws, no radiation) and **RT** (radiographic — records, best for pressure vessels, requires access and safety controls).
- **Mechanical**: bend tests, macro-etch (see the fusion zone), hardness traverses, and **coupon tests** per code.

Quality classes (e.g. ISO 5817 for fusion welds) grade acceptable imperfection levels — a class B (stringent) weld on a crane beam vs class D (lenient) on a cosmetic enclosure. The inspection level must match the component risk class; specifying RT-grade quality on a cosmetic bracket is paying for nothing. Feed weld failures into the [[quality-control-and-spc|quality]] loop — weld defects repeat until the process changes.

keyTakeaways: Pick the process by material, thickness, position, environment, and rate: TIG quality, MIG volume, SMAW portability, FCAW thick outdoor.
Weld symbols on the drawing (reference line, arrow side, size, length) fully define the joint — read and write them fluently.
Control heat input H = V·I/v, preheat by carbon equivalent, and manage distortion with balanced sequences, clamps, and minimum weld metal.
Inspection escalates VT → PT/MT → UT/RT; match the NDT class to the component risk.
